html:
A civil war in Lebanon from 1975 to 1990, fought between militias of its religious communities and drawn into the conflicts of its neighbours. It killed somewhere around 120,000 to 150,000 people and ruined Beirut, once the banking and holiday centre of the Arab world.

Lebanon's politics rested on the National Pact of 1943, which shared out power by religion and gave Maronite Christians the presidency. By the 1970s Muslims had grown in number and wanted a bigger share. Palestinian fighters had also moved in from Jordan after 1970 and used Lebanon as a base against Israel. In April 1975 a Christian militia attacked a bus carrying Palestinians, and fighting spread. Beirut was split along a "Green Line" between a Christian east and a Muslim west.

Foreign powers joined in. Syria sent troops in 1976 and stayed until 2005. Israel invaded in 1978 and again in 1982, besieging Beirut and forcing the Palestinian leadership out. Its Christian allies then massacred Palestinian refugees at Sabra and Shatila. Hezbollah, a Shia militia backed by Iran, rose in the south. American and French peacekeepers were bombed in 1983.

The Taif Agreement of 1989 rebalanced power, and the fighting ended in 1990. Hundreds of thousands left the country, adding to the long Lebanese emigration. The Baalbeck festival fell silent for over twenty years, while the singer Fairuz became a voice of a shared Lebanon above the factions.
